### Proliferation of subsea power cable and its impact on the copper industry _page 2_ 

Subsea cable technology has existed since the early 19<sup>th</sup> century, but the commercial proliferation of submarine power transmission has only come to prominence in the past five years. The industry is still young compared to its land-based power cable counterpart, but recent developments suggest that it has the potential to support the cable industry and enable significant growth in copper consumption from new applications. In this edition we investigate how this market is changing and what the implications are for the copper industry. 

<u>www.cruonline.crugroup.com</u> COPPER STUDIES September 2012 

2 

###### Early successes: Communication 

Submerging cables underwater is an old concept.  For over one hundred years since the first cable was positioned and used to transmit telegraph signals across New York Harbour in 1842, copper was the medium of choice for conducting telegraphy and then telephony signals under rivers and seas.  However, by the 1970’s and with telephonic bandwidth demand escalating, most trans-ocean communication was routed via satellites as submarine copper coaxial cables were prohibitively expensive to lay.  Sections of cable, of a maximum length of 9km, had to be jointed with repeaters or amplifiers to achieve minimum standards of servi

ce. The development of fibre optic cables in the late 1970-80’s led to huge leaps in the bandwidth capacity of communication cables, displacing the submarine copper coaxial cable market. This greatly reduced the copper unit intensity within submarine cables, as the metal was quite literally no longer at the core of the product, its role had been volumetrically reduced to providing a medium for the transmission of power for in-line repeaters. This came in the form of a thin copper tube or winding of copper strip. Telegraphy and telephony cables
Fibreoptic cables
###### Slow development: Power ###### HVDC While telecommunications demand for subsea cable developed at a terrific pace through the 20th century as gaps in international communication were bridged, power transmission via underwater cable developed at a much slower rate. The earliest recorded installation of a subsea power cable was in 1811 in Germany and was insulated with guta percha (a natural rubber that decays in air). Following the development of oil-impregnated insulation, early applications included the connection of offshore facilities such as lighthouses and infirmary ships, which required only low voltage cable laid across short distances. The range of uses for subsea power cables did expand to include high voltage, near-shore island connections but the type of routes that subsea power cables could serve were severely limited by losses due to the reliance on alternating current (AC) power. High voltage direct current (HVDC) cables are much more efficient in long distance power transmission but the technology was only rarely used and remained in its infancy during most of the 20th century. There were more technical challenges to overcome in the development of HVDC systems compared to HVAC and medium voltage DC (MVDC). The key concern here was in how to effectively convert the current to and from AC, which is the common way in which power is transmitted and distributed in local, land networks. Research performed in Sweden by **ASEA** (later to become **ABB** ) in the 1930’s led to a pivotal innovation in 1933, the high voltage mercury-arc valve. Continued development and testing of the equipment eventually led to the realisation of the Gotland transmission link, a 100kV rated, 98km working connection between Vдstervik, mainland Sweden and Ygne on the island of Gotland. The system could carry up to 20MW and was completed in 1954. The successful operation of the Gotland interconnector combined with the known benefits of using DC power over large distances led some power utility operators to invest in the technology despite its infancy. Through the course of the 1960’s ASEA commissioned four new subsea HVDC interconnector systems and **English Electric** (later to become **GEC** , and eventually **ALSTO

M** ) also installed a subsea HVDC link. Over the next few decades HVDC subsea projects grew in popularity and CRU’s analysis shows that 47 fully commissioned HVDC systems between 1954 and 2011 included subsea cables sections. Europe leads the way, but Asia has also been investing steadily

Over the course of this developmental stage for HVDC the power transfer capacity of subsea systems rose markedly and likewise did the cable voltage ratings and copper conductor thicknesses in order to meet these higher demands (see the chart on the following page). Key advances were again made in the ACDC rectifying technology, which initially limited subsea power transmission capacity to 600MW in the 1960’s but rose to a record-setting 2000MW in 1985 as fast-switching thyristors replaced outdated mercury-arc valve systems. To enable this expansion in converter power transmission capacity sometimes ‘bipolar’ DC cable arrangements were adopted which doubled the number of copper cores in the links (two cables at equal but opposite voltages; doubling the power transfer capacity compared to www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES September 2012 4 monopole designs). In this way, as conductors grew in size and number, so did the quantity of copper in HVDC systems. Cable power capacities increase, requiring thicker cables and

It is clear from the above chart that Northern Europe has dominated demand of HVDC cable throughout its history, representing 75% of the global figure by copper conductor weight. This greater intensity of use is attributed to geography as well as inhomogeneous distribution and timing of power generation and consumption across Northern Europe. Although high voltage subsea cable installations in Northern Europe found their initial use in providing bulk power from the Swedish national grid to a far-shore island, this source of demand for HVDC systems has actually been quite minimal in Northern Europe. Far greater use has emanated from integrating international energy markets as 17 out of the total 25 commissioned power ties have been for this purpose, with only 5 for the purpose of connecting far-shore islands and 3 for other purposes (connecting asynchronous and geographically distant national power grids and more recently for connecting an offshore oil platform and also to connect an offshore windfarm). ###### **Other types of subsea power cable** High voltage alternating current (HVAC) submarine power systems also exist and are often used for short distance and low power connections. This means that these projects would have to be vastly more numerous than those of HVDC to account for near-equivalent copper conductor tonnages. The reasons for operators favouring HVDC over HVAC are technical in origin but economic in practice. The disadvantages of alternative current for application in subsea cables are: - Alternating current power transmission requires three cores of cable, whereas DC requires only one (see the diagram below). - Alternating current incurs ‘reactive’ losses in addition to ‘resistive’ losses whereas direct current power transmission only suffers from resistive losses. - The significance of the reactive loss is more pronounced in underwater environments. - Cables are designed to handle a peak voltage, in AC systems this is 43% higher than the average voltage because the current is a sine wave, whereas in DC systems the peak voltage is the same as the average voltage. This means that for the same cable dimensions, an AC cable can carry 43% less power than a DC variant. DC powerlines on the other hand have the following drawbacks: - Difficulty in voltage stepping and changing between alternating current and direct current means DC systems require costly converters, whereas AC systems use relatively inexpensive transformers. A commonly held view after accounting for all of the above facts is that subsea HVAC lines are limited to a maximum of 80km, at longer route lengths AC cable costs are greater than the capital costs to build and operate converter stations, making HVDC a more affordable option

. In practice, however, while there are very rarely any HVAC lines which exceed this threshold distance, there are many examples of HVDC systems with shorter route lengths. This is often due to the technology’s application in bridging asynchronous grids i.e. power grids which operate AC at different frequencies (usually 50 or 60Hz). Other factors affecting the distance threshold of applicability for HVDC are, improving converter technology and new, lighter, cheaper subsea HVDC cable (branded HVDC-light by ABB), both of which reduce capital costs and make HVDC more affordable at lower power levels and distances. www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES September 2012 6 There is very little use of medium voltage DC subsea power cables (CRU classifies this as greater than 1kV but less than 60kV) as the cost to convert to DC is usually only applicable for larger distance transmission where it is more favourable to use higher voltage cable to reduce resistive losses. Medium voltage AC subsea power cable finds application over short distances for low power loads, making their equivalent copper demand very small compared with higher voltage subsea power cables. HVDC overhead and submarine cable transmission use fewer cables
© 2012 CRU International Limited confidential
###### **Applications and prospects for subsea power cable:** ###### **Grid interconnections:** The original application of submarine power cable concerned the transmission of electrical power across waterways for remote consumers e.g. islands that used autonomous power sources such as diesel generators. Its role soon expanded to include international electricity transmission connections for the exchange of bulk power e.g. the cross-channel project. The charts in the preceding sections indicate the extent of this demand historically (excluding AC interconnections, which are believed to be a fraction of the significance of DC lines due to their short route length). Below is a table that shows the potential demand for grid interconnections through to 2019 based around project proposals and their current development status. This aggregate line length does include some AC interconnections from 2010 onwards that we have visibility on, however these account for a total core length of 3,000km, meaning that the AC component of this market only comprises 13%. The principal driver of increasing grid interconnector demand is the integration of electrical power markets. As large amounts of electricity cannot be stored economically at present, nations with surplus electricity generation see no advantage in having excess supply unless they are connected to areas in deficit of electricity. While this demonstrates the concept, in reality it is rarely the case that a nation _continually_ produces an excess of electricity. Much more common is that a nation generates too much electricity on an intermittent

basis, as with hydro-power generating more electricity in periods of high rainfall. Analogous patterns occur in electricity consumption where nations experience peak demand at differing times during the day due to international time differences and cultural preferences. Intermittent supply and fluctuations in demand can be better balanced by market integration, which is effected by subsea power links where waterways separate grids. As mentioned in the prior section, Europe has consumed more subsea DC cable than other regions and CRU believes that this is a function of Europe’s development of many separate grids with unique generation and demand characteristics. In this way, there has been more opportunity to balance power supply and demand in Europe through the use of interconnections. Europe has also benefitted from a close proximity to visible success of interconnector development and use. This application is now commonplace in Northern Europe. Also, with a high number of installed routes, also comes additional demand for upgrading the links’ power-carrying capacity as electrical consumption/generation increases. In the future, this application appears set to expand rapidly, with average growth of 30% y-o-y from 2010 to 2014, declining to 12% y-o-y from 2015 to 2019. Europe will continue to dominate subsea cable demand for grid interconnection in this forecast period accounting for 72% of the projects (in terms of route length), with the Americas comprising 19% and Asia with 9%. Demand in the Americas resides entirely in North America within this forecast period, however, with the only subsea route options being coastal routes or connections to Hawaii, potential demand from the USA and Canada is unlikely to reach European levels. Asia is at a fledgling stage of subsea interconnector market development, with project proposals more focused upon connecting islands in southeast Asia to parent nation grids, rather than international market integration. Historically, links here have been mostly catered for by HVAC and MVAC subsea power cables (dependent upon the offshore power generation capacity). However, the number of fully commissioned offshore windfarms globally is actually quite low (approximately 65) and almost all of these have been near-shore, meaning that they have not contributed to significant cable demand. Furthermore, of the 65 offshore windfarms that CRU is aware are ful

ly commissioned, 33 are of low power or demonstration grade (<30MW power generation), which means that the copper conductor weight used in these link cables will be significantly less than that which serves a larger power source.  Wind power has been the primary type of offshore power generation, with only a few demonstration wave power facilities in existence.  Only a handful of 30MW+ windfarms were officially opened between 2005 and 2009, with the majority having been opened in the last two years, in this way, CRU has considered the subsea cable length for 2005 to 2009 to be negligible.

We have assigned a commissioning date within the 2010 to 2014 date range to all of the windfarm projects currently under construction or at late stage of permitting.  80% of the subsea core length of those projects which are at an earlier stage of permitting or are still being planned have been assigned to the 2015-2019 commissioning date range.  The results of this classification are shown in the table below which aggregates the expected subsea cable core length of all the projects within each date range.  It is clear that there is huge underlying demand for offshore links; potentially outstripping grid interconnector demand by 93% between 2010 and 2014. 

There is a far greater proportion of HVAC and MVAC used in offshore links than with grid interconnections.  Between 2010 and 2014 AC cable links account for 11,950km or 76% of the total. However, we project 10,650km of offshore AC cable links will be installed in between 2015 and 2019, or 57% of the total, representing weakening demand for this type of cable.  Early generation windfarms tend to be being built close to the shore and in smaller arrays, which generate less power.  This combination of attributes affords itself well to the use of MV and HVAC cables.  However, successive generation projects are tending toward more ambitious far-shore installations, where multiple windfarms are combined into 1GW+ windparks.  Linking these windparks to onshore substations is more economical and wastes less power with HVDC cabling.  In such systems offshore AC/DC converter stations must be provisioned in order to receive AC power from the windfarm transformer cabinet and to step-up the voltage for offshore-onshore DC transmission.  It is important to note that the numbers in the chart below account for the subsea route lengths from the coast to the windfarm transformer cabinet, this means that the subsea array cabling which connects turbine-transformer is excluded.

However, framing these quantities within the context of our global refined copper consumption forecasts reveals that the subsea power cable sector will account for less than 0.5% of demand from 2010 to 2019. We also recognise that the vast majority of this demand is forecast to stem from Europe, but even if the total copper tonnages listed in the chart above were entirely consumed within Europe, that would still represent less than 2% of European refined copper demand. An important side note is that the above figures do not include intrawindfarm cabling. CRU estimates that array cabling can reach up to 75km for large windfarms with only one transformer cabinet. The actual amount has not been modelled within this study. However, the average distance to shore of the windfarms that have been or are planned to be commissioned between 2010 and 2019, is 41km. CRU therefore would expect a maximum addition of 100% of the offshore power copper conductor core weights given above after the inclusion of array cabling. ###### **Disruptions (actual & potential) & risks:** These high voltage submarine power lines are not without disruptions and risks, however. Their location means that routine maintenance work is more difficult and costly, leading to a higher risk of technical failures, while the environment of the sea floor, wildlife and shipping activities can all cause damage to the lines. Other factors act to deter projects from being developed, such as environmental concerns and, more pressingly, long lead times for equipment which is leading to bottlenecks in development. © 2012 CRU International Limited confidential
###### **Faults** We categorise faults into three main segments; natural; technical; and third-party faults. Natural faults can occur due to movements of the sea floor, such as earthquakes or the movement of sediment, interference from large sea creatures such as whales, and problems induced by strong underwater currents. Cables can be forced by strong currents to vibrate, causing increased wear and tear over time, enhancing the risk of failure. www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES September 2012 10 Technical faults are obviously caused by equipment malfunctions and/or human mistakes made at some point during development, construction or maintenance. Problems at the planning stage and equipment malfunctions are no m

ore common than in other industrial undertakings, but the submarine location means that maintenance and testing is more difficult and expensive than other types of high voltage cables, leading to greater risks of technical failure.  Besides breakages, transmission problems can also occur when moisture is able to seep into the connectors. 

Third party faults typically manifest themselves as cable damage due to the activities of passing ships. Fishing trawler nets and dropped anchors being dragged along the sea bed are the main problems, as they can become ensnared in the cables and wrench them from their fastenings, exposing the cables to greater chances of fatigue failure.  In a number of cases, anchors and nets have also been known to snap the cables in two. 

###### **Environmental concerns** 

As the accompanying chart indicates, since the early days of submarine cables the activities and behaviour of large marine creatures such as whales have led to breakages caused by entanglements. While these have become less common since the mid-20<sup>th</sup> century, cables are still occasionally severed by being bitten in two – most likely by sharks. 

Besides the disruptions caused, many environmental campaigners are concerned by the effects of the cables on wildlife.  The sperm whale entanglements recorded prior to the 1960’s resulted in injuries and deaths, and typically occurred at the site of repairs, where additional cable had been left slack, allowing it to coil.  Deaths and entanglements have dwindled significantly since then, as technology has changed: Cables are now more frequently laid in trenches rather than on the sea bed, and they are designed to avoid coiling when slack. 

There are also concerns that the electromagnetic fields generated by the cables may disrupt or disorientate whales and other sea life, but there is currently no evidence that this is taking place.  Environmental campaigners continue to monitor the situation, however, and any if any proof arises that submarine HV cables are damaging sea life then this would lead to significant opposition to new projects, particularly in the developed world. 

###### **Supply bottlenecks** 

Despite the aforementioned analysis which forecast the market size for subsea power cable through to 2019, CRU expects that a significant proportion of this consumption will not occur in that time horizon due to supply bottlenecks.  Of all the disruptions listed, these are the main obstructions to further developments in this sector, and will severely impinge upon the attributable demand for refined copper from the subsea power cable industry.
